title: Twenty-Three Parties Showed Up to Challenge the BJP. The One That Didn't May Matter More.
excerpt: The INDIA bloc's first formal meeting since the 2024 elections delivered a five-point agenda — and exposed the cracks the opposition cannot afford.
body:
Twenty-three opposition parties gathered in New Delhi on Sunday for the first formal meeting of the INDIA bloc since the 2024 Lok Sabha elections — a show of unity that was immediately undercut by the one party that chose not to show up.

The DMK, which runs Tamil Nadu and is the bloc's most powerful southern ally, boycotted the meeting after a public breakdown in its relationship with the Congress. The absence was conspicuous enough that BJP leaders spent the evening mocking the coalition's shrinking footprint. "At this rate, by the third or fourth meeting, I suspect they will be holding it inside a car," said BJP MP Praveen Khandelwal.

## What Was on the Table

Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge opened the session at Constitution Club with a blunt assessment: the INDIA bloc must strengthen unity to confront what he described as the Modi government's misgovernance across political, economic, social and foreign policy fronts.

The agenda covered a wide arc — the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls (which the opposition claims is disenfranchising millions), alleged misuse of investigative agencies against opposition politicians, rising prices, weak investment, unemployment, examination paper leaks, and what Kharge called the Centre's "weak" foreign policy.

Flanked by Rahul Gandhi, Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav and other senior leaders at a joint press conference afterwards, Kharge announced five key decisions. The bloc will write to the Chief Justice of India about the electoral roll revision and what it described as "vote loot." It unanimously demanded the immediate resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-CBSE examination controversy. And it called on the government to convene an all-party meeting to discuss what it termed the "precarious economic situation" — citing India's slip from the world's fourth to sixth-largest economy, the rupee's fall to a record 95 against the dollar, and rising fuel prices.

## Mamata's Bombshell

West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee used the platform to air a grievance that has been festering since the state assembly elections: she alleged that the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision exercise had favoured the BJP, effectively helping it win power in her state after 15 years of Trinamool Congress rule.

The charge is incendiary. If taken seriously by the Supreme Court or any independent inquiry, it would raise fundamental questions about the integrity of India's electoral infrastructure. For now, it remains an allegation — but one that the broader opposition coalition appears willing to echo.

## The Cracks

For all the headline unity, the fractures were visible. The DMK's boycott followed a breakdown with Congress over political developments in Tamil Nadu. The CPI(M) raised objections to Congress's campaign rhetoric in Kerala. And several regional parties privately expressed frustration over seat-sharing arrangements and what they see as Congress's reluctance to be "large-hearted" with coalition partners.

Rahul Gandhi acknowledged the tensions directly. "As the biggest party here, we will have all the love and affection to unite this team," he said, according to leaders present at the meeting.

The bloc decided to meet every two months, with the next session scheduled for Hyderabad in August.

## The BJP Response

The ruling party was swift and dismissive. BJP Rajya Sabha MP Ghulam Ali Khatana questioned the relevance of the entire exercise, while Khandelwal called it "a group of disappointed people" trying to regroup after repeated electoral defeats.

"This is not an alliance, because in an alliance all parties move together. Here, every party is working separately," Khandelwal said.

## Why NRIs Should Care

For the Indian diaspora, the INDIA bloc meeting matters less for what was decided than for what it reveals about the state of Indian democracy. A 23-party opposition coalition that cannot keep its most important southern ally in the room faces structural challenges that no joint press conference can paper over.

At the same time, the substance of the opposition's critique — that the economy is sliding, elections may be compromised, and the government is using investigative agencies against political rivals — touches on questions that matter to anyone with a stake in India's institutional health. Whether the INDIA bloc can translate these grievances into political outcomes, rather than periodic meetings, is the question that will define Indian opposition politics for the rest of this decade.
